prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Artillery shells slammed into a hospital Sunday in the northern Sri Lankan district of Mullaittivu, where civilians -- including a growing number of children -- are being treated as government forces and Tamil rebels continue to clash. A Sri Lankan soldier walks through Mullaittivu, the former military headquarters of the Tamil rebels. More than 200 civilians and at least 30 children have been injured in the last three days of fighting, a relief worker told CNN Sunday. "That is the absolute minimum (number of injured)," the aid worker, who did not want to be identified for fear of jeopardizing the work of relief organizations, said. Government officials are accusing aid organizations and foreign media of sensationalizing civilian casualties. "It looks as if it's convenient for certain agencies to exaggerate the numbers so that this can be converted to a humanitarian crisis in the public eye, " Secretary of Foreign Affairs Dr. Palitha Kohona told CNN. On Sunday, Sri Lankan Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa promised to "continue with the military offensive until we liberate the remaining area under LTTE (the rebel group) control," according to Sri Lanka's state-run news agency.  Watch a report on civilians caught in fighting » . A "handful" of United Nations staff are working around the clock to save a growing number of children caught in the crossfire, a U.N. spokesman said Saturday. Children as young as 4 months old were being treated in local hospitals for shrapnel injuries and other "wounds of war," spokesman James Elder told CNN. "There is just intense fighting in a small area where children and other civilians are," Elder said. "The space (where conflict is taking place) is shrinking and the fighting is augmenting." Thursday, U.N. aid workers rescued 50 critically injured children and 105 adults, he said. "We are trying to get as many people out of there as we can," Elder said. Humanitarian groups say as many as 250,000 unprotected civilians are trapped in the area. Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has promised to allow safe passage to trapped civilians and urged the Tamil Tigers to promise the same. "We have declared a safe zone for civilians, the coordinates of which were announced by the security forces," Rajapaksa said on his government's Web site. "It is unfortunate that the (Tamil Tiger group) is exploiting this declared safe zone for civilians by placing their heavy artillery within the safe zone and using it as a launching pad to attack security forces and indiscriminately kill civilians." The fighting has created a "nightmarish" situation for civilians in the conflict zone, Elder said. An emerging shortage of humanitarian supplies and diminished access to clean water, sanitation, and food are compounding a crisis, he said. Sunday, Sri Lankan soldiers seized a key rebel stronghold in a surprise attack deep in Tamil held territory. Troops crossed a lagoon and entered the town of Mullaittivu before encountering heavy resistance from Tamil fighters, according to the government-run news agency. The The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) -- commonly known as the Tamil Tigers -- have fought for an independent homeland for the country's ethnic Tamil minority since 1983. The civil war has left more than 70,000 people dead.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Artillery shells struck a hospital Sunday in Sri Lanka’s northern district of Mullaittivu, where civilians—including a growing number of children—are being treated as government forces and Tamil rebels continue to clash.

A Sri Lankan soldier walks through Mullaittivu, the former military headquarters of the Tamil rebels.

More than 200 civilians, including at least 30 children, have been injured during the past three days of fighting, a relief worker told CNN on Sunday.

“That is the absolute minimum number of injured,” said the aid worker, who requested anonymity out of concern that being identified could jeopardize the work of relief organizations.

Government officials have accused aid organizations and foreign media outlets of sensationalizing civilian casualties.

“It looks as if it’s convenient for certain agencies to exaggerate the numbers so that this can be converted into a humanitarian crisis in the public eye,” Secretary of Foreign Affairs Dr. Palitha Kohona told CNN.

On Sunday, Sri Lankan Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa promised to “continue with the military offensive until we liberate the remaining area under LTTE [the rebel group] control,” according to Sri Lanka’s state-run news agency.

Watch a report on civilians caught in the fighting »

A “handful” of United Nations staff members are working around the clock to save a growing number of children caught in the crossfire, a U.N. spokesman said Saturday.

Children as young as 4 months old were being treated in local hospitals for shrapnel injuries and other “wounds of war,” spokesman James Elder told CNN.

“There is just intense fighting in a small area where children and other civilians are,” Elder said. “The space where the conflict is taking place is shrinking, and the fighting is intensifying.”

On Thursday, U.N. aid workers rescued 50 critically injured children and 105 adults, he said.

“We are trying to get as many people out of there as we can,” Elder said.

Humanitarian groups say as many as 250,000 unprotected civilians are trapped in the area.

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has promised to allow trapped civilians safe passage and has urged the Tamil Tigers to make the same commitment.

“We have declared a safe zone for civilians, the coordinates of which were announced by the security forces,” Rajapaksa said on his government’s website. “It is unfortunate that the [Tamil Tiger group] is exploiting this declared safe zone for civilians by placing its heavy artillery within the safe zone and using it as a launching pad to attack security forces and indiscriminately kill civilians.”

The fighting has created a “nightmarish” situation for civilians in the conflict zone, Elder said. An emerging shortage of humanitarian supplies, along with reduced access to clean water, sanitation, and food, is compounding the crisis, he added.

On Sunday, Sri Lankan soldiers seized a key rebel stronghold in a surprise attack deep inside Tamil-held territory. Troops crossed a lagoon and entered the town of Mullaittivu before encountering heavy resistance from Tamil fighters, according to the government-run news agency.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE)—commonly known as the Tamil Tigers—have fought since 1983 for an independent homeland for the country’s ethnic Tamil minority. The civil war has left more than 70,000 people dead.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Sunday, artillery fire struck a hospital in Mullaittivu, a district in northern Sri Lanka where civilians—including an increasing number of children—were receiving treatment as clashes continued between government troops and Tamil rebels.

A Sri Lankan soldier was seen walking through Mullaittivu, which had served as the Tamil rebels’ military headquarters.

A relief worker told CNN on Sunday that more than 200 civilians, including at least 30 children, had been wounded during the previous three days of combat. The worker, who requested anonymity out of concern that identification could endanger relief organizations’ operations, said those figures represented “the absolute minimum.”

Sri Lankan officials have accused humanitarian agencies and international news organizations of overstating civilian casualty numbers. Foreign Affairs Secretary Dr. Palitha Kohona told CNN that some organizations appeared to find it useful to inflate the figures in order to portray the situation publicly as a humanitarian emergency.

According to Sri Lanka’s state-operated news service, Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa vowed Sunday that the military campaign would continue until the final territory controlled by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, had been freed.

Watch a report about civilians trapped in the fighting »

A U.N. spokesperson said Saturday that a small number of United Nations personnel were working continuously to help the rising number of children caught between the opposing forces. Spokesman James Elder told CNN that hospitals in the area were treating children as young as four months for shrapnel injuries and other war-related wounds.

Elder described severe combat taking place within a confined area occupied by children and other civilians. He said the conflict zone was becoming smaller while the intensity of the fighting was increasing.

On Thursday, U.N. relief personnel evacuated 50 children with critical injuries and 105 adults, Elder said. He added that aid workers were attempting to remove as many people as possible.

Humanitarian organizations estimate that as many as 250,000 civilians without protection remain trapped in the region. Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa pledged to provide them with a secure route out and called on the Tamil Tigers to make the same commitment.

In a statement posted on the government’s website, Rajapaksa said authorities had established a civilian safety zone and that security forces had publicly released its coordinates. He accused the Tamil Tigers of taking advantage of the zone by positioning heavy artillery inside it, using the area as a base for attacks on government forces, and killing civilians indiscriminately.

Elder characterized conditions for people inside the battle zone as “nightmarish.” He said the situation was being worsened by a developing shortage of humanitarian aid and reduced access to food, sanitation, clean water, and other essential supplies.

Also on Sunday, Sri Lankan troops captured an important rebel position during an unexpected operation far inside Tamil-controlled territory. According to the state-run news agency, soldiers crossed a lagoon and moved into Mullaittivu before facing strong resistance from Tamil combatants.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam—widely called the Tamil Tigers—have been fighting since 1983 to establish an independent homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority. More than 70,000 people have died in the civil war.
outputs.L3:
Artillery shells struck a hospital in Sri Lanka’s northern Mullaittivu district as fighting intensified between government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). The attack heightened concerns about civilians caught in the shrinking conflict zone, where access to medical care and humanitarian assistance was increasingly limited.

A relief worker reported that more than 200 civilians, including at least 30 children, had been injured over three days of clashes. United Nations personnel were working to evacuate the most critically wounded, among them infants suffering from shrapnel injuries. Humanitarian organizations estimated that as many as 250,000 civilians remained trapped in the area.

Sri Lankan government officials disputed accounts of the scale of civilian suffering, accusing aid agencies and foreign media outlets of exaggerating casualty figures in an effort to depict the military campaign as a humanitarian crisis. At the same time, the country’s defense secretary pledged that the offensive would continue until government forces had captured all territory still controlled by the LTTE.

The worsening violence, mounting casualties and difficulty of evacuating the injured underscored the growing danger faced by civilians as the military advanced farther into the rebels’ remaining strongholds.
outputs.L4:
Artillery fire struck a hospital in Sri Lanka’s northern Mullaittivu district as fighting intensified between government troops and the separatist Tamil Tiger rebels, worsening an already severe humanitarian emergency in the region.

Aid workers and United Nations personnel said they witnessed casualties at the hospital and helped evacuate critically wounded patients. Medical staff continued treating civilians under increasingly difficult conditions, with limited supplies and little protection from the fighting. The Sri Lankan government disputed some accounts from the conflict zone, saying reports of casualties and attacks were exaggerated, while independent verification remained difficult because access for journalists and relief organizations was tightly restricted.

More than 200 civilians were reported injured over three days, including at least 30 children. Relief officials warned that hospitals and temporary medical facilities were struggling to cope with the steady arrival of wounded people.

The violence came as government forces advanced into territory held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. Their offensive compressed the fighting into an increasingly small area where large numbers of civilians had sought refuge. Humanitarian agencies estimated that as many as 250,000 people remained trapped, with few safe routes out and limited access to food, medicine, clean water and shelter.

Both sides faced growing international concern over civilian safety. Aid agencies called for the wounded to be evacuated, relief supplies to be allowed into the area and hospitals and other civilian sites to be protected. As the battlefield continued to shrink, officials warned that further shelling could cause even heavier civilian casualties and deepen the humanitarian crisis.

Correspondents described how long-range weapons can influence battlefield strategy while also posing serious risks to civilians and critical infrastructure. The segment included analysis from military experts and emphasized the importance of verifying information from conflict zones.

counterfactuals.prompt: Find a news report describing civilian and child casualties during the 2009 fighting between Sri Lankan government forces and the Tamil Tigers.
counterfactuals.output:
A relevant report is:

**BBC News, “Sri Lanka civilians ‘die in shelling’,” 10 May 2009**  
https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/south_asia/8043169.stm

The report cited a doctor in the Tamil Tiger–held conflict zone who said **at least 378 civilians, including more than 100 children, were killed**, and over 1,100 people were wounded during heavy shelling. The Sri Lankan government denied shelling the designated civilian “safe zone,” so the casualty claims were disputed and difficult to verify independently.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What did CNN report when Sri Lankan troops seized the LTTE stronghold of Mullaittivu and humanitarian groups warned that up to 250,000 civilians were trapped?
counterfactuals.output:
CNN reported on January 25, 2009, that Sri Lankan forces had captured Mullaittivu, the Tamil Tigers’ last major stronghold, after advancing into the northeastern town. President Mahinda Rajapaksa described the seizure as a decisive step toward defeating the LTTE.

The report also highlighted humanitarian warnings that as many as 250,000 civilians were trapped in the shrinking conflict zone, exposed to shelling and with limited access to food, medicine, and evacuation routes. CNN noted that the claims and battlefield conditions were difficult to verify independently because journalists and most aid workers were barred from the area.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
The article is an **Associated Press** report by **Ravi Nessman**, published **February 2, 2009**, under the headline:

**“Hospital shelled in Sri Lanka war zone, 9 killed”**

It reports the shelling of the hospital at **Puthukkudiyiruppu in Mullaittivu District**, UNICEF/U.N. negotiations to evacuate wounded children, and the Sri Lankan military’s continuing offensive against the LTTE. The story was widely republished by outlets including NBC News and Fox News, sometimes under slightly altered headlines.
